attempts.summary: Implemented cron access control on node1 (Alpine) via Ansible run from node2, the only Ansible-equipped node, used as control node. Alpine's cron stack is BusyBox crond/crontab, which has no /etc/cron.allow or /etc/cron.deny support (confirmed via strings on /bin/busybox and the setuid helper /bin/bbsuid). Since crontab is a symlink to bbsuid and dispatch happens purely on argv[0] with no path validation, the only real enforcement point is bbsuid's own execute permission (a wrapper on the crontab symlink alone is bypassable via `exec -a crontab /bin/bbsuid`, which was verified empirically). The Ansible playbook creates an opsadmin user, a cronusers group containing root and opsadmin, restricts /bin/bbsuid to mode 4750 owned root:cronusers, keeps /etc/crontabs root-owned/non-writable, and ensures crond is enabled. Verified that root and opsadmin can schedule cron jobs while an unauthorized user (alpine) is blocked both via the crontab command and via direct spool-file writes. Completed the mandatory restart protocol on both node1 and node2, one at a time, proving boot_id changed and full recovery of cron service, permission state, and Ansible connectivity after each restart.
